To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the degradation of benzane in complex biofilm communities from an aerated wastewater treatment pond was dominated by phylotypes related with Betaproteobacteriaceae and that the initial ring attack is likely to occur by dioxygenase-mediated hydroxylation of benzene.

the benzene-degrading community of an aerated textile treatment pond is dominated by phylotypes of Betaproteobacterial genera, and that the degradation of benzène occurs via dihydroxylation followed by meta-cleavage.

benzene is degraded in a complex microbial biofilm by a dihydroxygenation pathway with subsequent meta cleavage of catechol, and that the active biomass is composed of Betaproteobacterial phylotypes related, e.g., to Zoogloae, Ferribacterum, Aquabacterum and Hydrogenophagus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the predominant phylotypes involved in benzene degradation in a microbial biofilm and their functional assignment based on RNA and protein-SIP.
benzene degradation by complex microbial biofilms and provides a first detailed analysis of the structure, function, activity, and pathways of the involved bacteria

a comprehensive characterization of the active microbial community in an aerated pond containing textile waste and the identification of the predominant pathways involved in benzene degradation under oxic conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a complex microbial community consisting of Betaproteobacterial phylotypes performs the initial ring attack on benzene by dihydroxylation, which is followed by meta-cleavage.
benzene is initially dihydroxylated and then degraded by meta-cleavage, and that the Betaproteboacteria are the major benzene-degrading bacteria in the studied biofilms.
a complex microbial community is involved in benzene degradation in the studied aerobic treatment system, with the phylotypes identified in this study being key players.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the identified phylotypes performed distinct functions related to the degradation of benzane, and the degradation of benzne in complex microbial biofilm is dominated by a dihydroxylating pathway with subsequent meta cleavage of catechol.

the identified bacterial phylotypes are able to perform benzene degradation in the investigated system, but the contribution of each phylotype to benzene degradation and the exact pathways are still unclear.
a complex microbial community degrades benzene by a meta-cleavage pathway, with the Betaproteo-bacteria being the most important phylum involved in this process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

RNA-SIP can be used to identify active members in a complex microbial community, and that RNA-SIP and compound-specific stable isotopic analysis can be combined with metaproteomic approaches to elucidate the function of the active biomass.
RNA- and protein-SIP are powerful tools to identify the structure and function of complex microbial communities involved in the degradation and metabolism of benzene in natural environments.

benzene degradation by complex microbial biofilm communities in an aerated treatment system can be investigated at a molecular level by using RNA- and protein-SIP and compound-specific stable isotopic analyses.
